1:
The opening phrase fixes nothing, and five say so differently. latin-fathers The Gloss takes it to mark the passage from one year’s preaching to another, after John’s death, when Jesus is already in all things spoken against. Augustine notes that the other two evangelists relate the same matter without the phrase, so Matthew may have preserved the order of time and they the order of recollection — unless the words mean an indefinite time. grammatical-historical Robertson says the paragraph opens as an earlier one does, with a word for a definite time we cannot fix. Ellicott finds the three arrangements so different that we are at sea in attempting a harmony, and can only regard the phrase as belonging to a separate history elsewhere. Lightfoot works instead from the other Gospel’s second-first sabbath: the sheaf of firstfruits was offered on the second day of Passover week, not the morrow after the weekly sabbath, and from that day seven weeks ran to Pentecost. Barnes reaches the same place and adds that barley is in full ear in early April; Clarke reproduces Lightfoot’s reckoning almost word for word. reformed Gill supposes them on the way to worship, the path lying through the fields.

Whether the sabbath was broken is the second question. Chrysostom puts it sharpest: why lead them through the cornfields on the sabbath, knowing all things, unless he desired to break it? He desired it indeed, but not absolutely, and broke it not without cause but furnished a sufficient reason, causing the Law to cease and yet not offending against it — pleading natural necessity to soften the Jews, since in things manifestly sinful no excuse serves, but here hunger delivers the disciples from all accusation. He bids us admire men so limited in desire that they despise the support of the flesh and will not go away from Christ. Ellicott locates the offence: the act was permitted so far as property went, but to pluck the ears was to reap and to rub the husks to thresh, so the new Teacher seemed to sanction a breach of the day. Augustine observes that the charge was sabbath-breaking and not theft, since the Law let a man take what he needed to eat, and that the two examples are drawn one from royal persons and one from priestly, so the charge attaches the less to him who is King and Priest; the plucking was permitted, he says, to convict the Manichaeans, who will not pull up a herb for fear of murder. Jerome recalls that the crowding had left them no food, and finds in the rubbing a proof of an austere life; on the defence he tells how David, flying from Saul, was given the consecrated loaves, the priest esteeming it better to deliver men from famine than to sacrifice, since the preservation of man is itself a sacrifice acceptable to God. puritan-evangelical Henry finds the teachers erring here in the opposite direction from their usual looseness, men of corrupt minds commonly thinking zeal in rituals atones for loose morals. Calvin says it more sharply: hypocrites take liberty in the weightiest matters and are exact in trifles, so one could scarcely move a finger without making the conscience tremble — though envy moved them more than superstition. Hilary reads it figuratively, the field being the world, the sabbath rest, the corn believers ripening for harvest, the hunger their desire for men’s salvation; Raban makes the plucking a withdrawing of men from the world, and adds that they walk the cornfields with the Lord who delight in the Scriptures and search what lies hid under the letter. Remigius takes the title Son of man to mean that he whom they suppose a mere man is Lord of the sabbath, and may change the law because he made it. wesleyan-arminian Wesley notes they took just what sufficed for present necessity.
2:
What made the plucking unlawful is set out most fully from the rabbis. grammatical-historical Lightfoot cites the traditions: he that reaps on the sabbath, though never so little, is guilty, and to pluck the ears is a kind of reaping; the Fathers of the Traditions reckon thirty-nine primitive works, with derivative works of the same rank, so that digging belongs with ploughing and plucking with reaping. Robertson states the same charge in a line, that plucking was reaping and rubbing was threshing, and adds that the critics were watching a chance and jumped at it. Barnes notes that on any other day the act was expressly permitted, so the whole complaint rests on the day. Ellicott places the accusers, who in the other Gospels belong to the company come down from Jerusalem to watch the new Teacher: he had claimed to forgive sins and eaten with publicans, and now they found him teaching men to dishonour the sabbath. wesleyan-arminian Clarke measures the superstition by its cost, since in their wars the Jews thought it a crime even to defend themselves on that day, and enemies who saw this deferred operations to it, which is how Jerusalem was taken; those who know not the spirit of the divine law, he adds, are often superstitious to inhumanity and indulgent to impiety, and a censorious spirit in religion is one of the greatest curses a man can fall under. reformed Gill notes that the watchers went along with him for the purpose of observing his words and actions.

What the appeal to David proves divides them. Calvin counts five arguments in the reply and takes this as the first: if David’s necessity excused him the same must be admitted for others, so the ceremonies of the Law are not violated where godliness is not infringed. But he insists on a premise the others pass over: Christ takes for granted that David was free from blame, since the Spirit commends the priest who gave him the holy bread; had David done what was contrary to law it would have been vain to plead his example, for what is prohibited to a particular end no necessity can make lawful. Wesley says the opposite in half a line, that necessity was a sufficient plea for David’s transgressing the law in a higher instance, and Robertson notes that David and his men did the very thing charged here, what was not lawful. Barnes draws the principle rather than the parallel: the act had passed uncondemned, and proved that in cases of necessity the laws did not bind a man, which all laws admit. Ellicott reads it as an argument from greater to less, made where the Pharisees thought themselves strongest — would they accuse David of sacrilege for setting aside a twofold law in urgent need, and if they shrank from that, was it not inconsistent to condemn these disciples for a far lighter transgression? Gill turns the question back on the questioners, since men who had not read the Scriptures were unfit either to teach or to censure others, and if they had read them they could not but have observed the case. Lightfoot fills in the history: the priest’s question why David came alone is comparative, set against the train that became a captain-general of Israel, for David came to Nob not as one fleeing but as one inquiring at the oracle by the king’s command, dissembling that he had sent his army ahead, and asking bread for the few trusty servants with him. He adds the rabbinic gloss that nothing may hinder the taking care of life but idolatry, adultery and murder — a passage Clarke reproduces almost word for word, with the comment that it would be lawful to eat even the loaf now set on, when no other is at hand and men are hunger-bitten.
4:
The two halves of the defence are a precedent and a standing practice. On the first, reformed Gill fixes the place, not the temple, which was not then built, but the tabernacle at Nob, the city of the priests. grammatical-historical Barnes describes the loaves laid on the table in the holy place to remain a week and then be eaten by the priests only, their place taken by fresh bread. Ellicott counts them, twelve in two rows of six, offered every sabbath day, the previous week’s loaves removed and reserved for the priests’ exclusive use; and he draws from the single instance the general principle, that when positive commands and necessities involving the good of man come into collision, the latter and not the former must prevail. wesleyan-arminian Wesley adds that the twelve represented the twelve tribes, and that the stale loaves were to be eaten by the priests only. Clarke gives the Hebrew name, bread of the presence or of faces, because it was set continually before the face of Jehovah.

The second argument is the harder, since it names the priests themselves as sabbath-breakers. Barnes sets out what their work involved: two lambs killed on the sabbath over and above the daily sacrifice, which meant slaying, skinning, preparing and burning, and the kindling of fires that the Law expressly forbade the people on that day; they did what in others would have profaned the sabbath, and were blameless, and did it in the temple itself, the place where the law should be most strictly kept. Gill lists the same servile works, the killing, flaying, cutting in pieces, laying on the altar, cutting of wood and kindling of fire. Clarke glosses the verb plainly, that to profane is to put the day to what might be called a common use. Ellicott says no one blamed the priests, for they were serving in the temple of Jehovah. Lightfoot supplies the maxim the argument turns on, quoting the rabbis to the effect that the servile work done in the holy things is not servile, that the same works done on other days were done also on the sabbath, and that there is no sabbatism at all in the temple. Calvin builds the conclusion. This is the argument, he says, by which Christ proves the alleged violation free from all blame, since it is lawful to slay beasts for sacrifice and to circumcise infants and to do the other things belonging to the worship of God, whence it follows that the duties of piety are in no degree inconsistent with one another. And he presses the comparison further than the rest: if the temple sanctifies manual operations connected with sacrifice and the whole outward service, then the holiness of the true and spiritual temple has greater efficacy still in exempting its worshippers from blame while they discharge the duties of godliness — the object the disciples had in view being to present to God souls consecrated by the Gospel. He also enters a caution about the word itself. Strictly, he says, the expression is not accurate but accommodated to the hearers, since when the Law enjoins men to abstain from their employments it does not forbid them to perform the services of religion; Christ admits as true what might appear so to persons who do not know how to judge and distinguish, and rests satisfied with proving that the labours performed in the temple are not offensive to God. Only Matthew glances at this argument, Calvin notes, the other evangelists passing it by.
6:
The three arguments of the preceding verses come to a head in a single claim: verse 6 asserts that something greater than the temple is present here. Albert Barnes and Adam Clarke both take the greatness to be Christ’s own, and therefore a claim to deity: if the temple sanctified the priests who profaned the sabbath in serving it, then the Lord of the temple sanctifies far more surely those who serve him. Charles Ellicott prefers the neuter reading, “here is something greater than the Temple,” and finds the greater thing in the body of the Son of Man as the truest temple, with a wider application still to the bodies of all men in whom God dwells. A.T. Robertson reports the alternatives without settling between them: the greater is Christ himself, or else the work and the disciples engaged in it outrank the building.

The argument from mercy in verse 7 is the one the commentators dwell on longest, because it turns the case from precedent to principle. John Calvin reads Hosea 6:6 comparatively rather than absolutely: God does not despise the external rites he himself appointed, but he values them only as they are directed to their proper object, and set beside deeds of kindness they are the lesser thing. He is careful to add that piety toward God outranks charity toward men as far as God outranks men; the comparison holds between ceremony and mercy, not between God and neighbour. John Wesley states the working rule in a sentence — when acts of mercy and acts of worship interfere with each other, he always prefers acts of mercy. Adam Clarke sets out four ways a positive law ceases to oblige: natural necessity, a superior particular law, the law of charity and mercy, and the express dispensation of the Lawgiver. John Gill and Charles Ellicott both press the charge in the second half of the verse: the fault of the Pharisees was not ignorance of the text but a use of it that condemned the guiltless.

The conclusion in verse 8 is read two ways. John Gill insists that the Son of Man is Christ and not man generally, since no man is lord of a divine institution. John Calvin distinguishes the two claims carefully: verse 6 asserts the personal holiness of Christ, while verse 8 asserts his authority to exempt his followers, so that the disciples are covered by their master’s right and not by their own. John Lightfoot supplies the long view in two parts: Adam kept the sabbath first under the law of nature, and only after the fall under a positive law, so the day was always subject to the Lawgiver rather than the reverse. Adam Clarke draws out the consequence the church later acted on, that the same lordship transferred the observance to the Lord’s day. John Wesley alone suspects a displacement in the text and suggests that verses 7 and 8 may have been transposed.
9:
A second sabbath scene follows, and the commentators first settle when it happened. Augustine notes that Matthew’s “when he had passed thence” means only that Jesus did not enter the synagogue before leaving the cornfield, and that Luke, who says plainly it was another sabbath, is free to supply the interval. John Gill and Charles Ellicott agree; Ellicott adds that Matthew and Mark leave the impression of the same day, and credits Luke with the more careful inquiry, placing the synagogue at Capernaum among the very Pharisees just reproved.

A second harmony problem follows. Matthew reports that the Pharisees put the question, while Mark and Luke report that Jesus put it to them. Augustine resolves it in sequence: they asked first; then, reading their intent to accuse, he set the man in the midst and asked them the counter-question of Luke 6:9; and when they held their peace he made the comparison of the sheep. Chrysostom fixes the motive rather than the order — they did not ask in order to learn but in order to accuse, and though the deed itself would have furnished the charge, they wanted a handle in his words as well.

On the substance, Jerome makes the reply an exposure of covetousness: men who would hurry to lift a fallen sheep out of a pit on the sabbath do it for their own property’s sake, and a man is much better than a sheep. The Gloss presses the same reversal — they profane the sabbath by works of covetousness who charge him with profaning it by works of charity — and reads “ye shall do no servile work” in Leviticus 23:3 as meaning no sin, since in the everlasting rest we shall rest from evil only. John Calvin draws the warning inward: minds ruled by hatred or pride turn light into darkness and will condemn a divine work outright, and undue weight on ceremony crowds out the weightier matters of Matthew 23:23.

The Latin readings turn the withered hand into a figure. Jerome sees it withered in the synagogue of the Jews until the Lord came, the right hand restored in the apostles who believed and given back to its former occupation. Hilary reads it the same way but for the Pharisees’ sake, the hand made like the apostles’ ministry of salvation, so that they should not resent that work being done by others when their own hand might be made able for it too. Raban widens it to the race, barren of good works since the hand was stretched out to the fruit of Genesis 3:6 and healed by the innocent hand stretched out on the cross; and since the hand is bid to stretch out first, he takes the cure of a barren mind to be liberality in almsgiving, the grasping right hand at last distributing freely. Raban also gives the plain reason Jesus works on sabbaths: not only the spiritual rest, but the gathering of the people. Matthew Henry keeps the figure but turns it to grace — by nature our hands are withered and we can do nothing good, and Christ heals the withered hand by putting life into the dead soul.
10:
The man’s condition is described medically and then rabbinically. John Gill takes the hand to be dry, the juices spent and the sinews contracted, useless to him; Luke specifies the right hand, and Gill extends the injury to the whole arm, citing a Talmudic case of an arm that withered and the report that the gospel used by the Nazarenes made the man a tradesman who lived by his hands. Albert Barnes and Adam Clarke both guess at palsy, Clarke at a partial paralysis, and Clarke adds the observation that the man’s feet were spared him, so that he could bring himself to public worship and be met there.

Whether the question was a question at all is the point at issue. John Lightfoot answers flatly that these are not the words of inquirers but of deniers, and produces the canons behind them: the healthy may not use physic on the sabbath; a man with a pain in his loins may anoint with oil but not with oil of roses; a man with the toothache may swallow vinegar but not spit it out; no wine in a sore eye. None of these touched a cure worked by a word only, but they gave a pretext to men already sworn to quarrel with him, especially the rule that whatever could have been done on the sabbath eve does not drive away the sabbath. Charles Ellicott reads two things as implied: that they expected him to heal, knowing that the sight of such suffering always moved him to act, and that they had already resolved to make the cure the ground of a formal charge before the local court of Matthew 5:21 — the casuistry allowed healing where life was at stake, and a permanent infirmity plainly was not. A.T. Robertson stays with the grammar, noting that the interrogative “if” is elliptical and imitates a Hebrew idiom. John Calvin answers the question by refusing it: they should first have asked whether restoring a withered hand by a word was a work of God or of man, since when God appointed the sabbath he laid down no law for himself, and it was excessive folly to prescribe rules for God and restrain the freedom of his operations.

The reply appeals to the questioners’ own practice. John Lightfoot supplies the governing canon, that tender care must be taken of an Israelite’s goods, with the rulings on a beast fallen into a ditch: feed it in the pit if it cannot be raised, or bring clothes and litter and bear it up; and the dispute of R. Lazar and R. Joshua over lifting a beast and its foal on a holy day. Adam Clarke reproduces the same canons and credits Lightfoot for them, then turns the point moral: self-interest is a very decisive casuist and removes abundance of scruples in a moment, always the first consulted and the most readily obeyed — not sinful to hear, but not fit to govern. Albert Barnes makes it an argument from the lesser to the greater that left them silent, and adds from Mark that Jesus looked on them with anger. John Calvin presses hardest: since sin is committed by neglect of duty as well as by transgression, there is little difference between manslaughter and refusing relief to a man in distress. He notes too that Christ does not here reason from his divinity as he does in John 5:18, because this single defence already refuted them.
12:
The comparison closes with a question rather than a rule. John Gill spells out the proportion: a rational creature is more excellent than an irrational one, so that even a man’s health outweighs a beast’s life; if it is lawful to feed a fallen sheep or lift it from a ditch, it is lawful to do good to men, and healing belongs among such acts of beneficence — the more so for a man who seems to have earned his bread by hand labour. Albert Barnes makes the same step from the brute to one made in the image of God, one for whom the Saviour came to die, and notes that the abstract principle was universally allowed among the Jews; Jesus only showed that the principle they already acted on applied with more force to the case in front of them, so that the deed was lawful by their own confession. Adam Clarke names the form of the argument — it is argumentum ad hominem, taking them on their own ground and confuting them from their own maxims and conduct — and then turns it on his own readers, who do more for a beast of burden or pleasure than for a man for whom Christ died. A.T. Robertson keeps the question open rather than answering it, calling it one of Christ’s pregnant questions that goes to the roots of things, one which Christian civilisation has not yet adequately answered.

The command that follows is read as a test case in obedience. Adam Clarke observes what the man might reasonably have said — make the hand whole first, and then I will stretch it out — and calls that reasonable-sounding plea foolishness in his case: faith disregards apparent impossibilities where there is a command and a promise, and the effort to believe is often the very faith by which the soul is healed. Albert Barnes presses the same lesson on the sinner, that a command is to be obeyed without first examining the question of ability, since God gives strength where there is a disposition to obey; but he guards it carefully, insisting that the passage proves nothing about the sinner’s power and must not be used as if it did. Charles Ellicott reads the obedience as itself the evidence: the tense shows the hand was restored in the very act of stretching it out, and a command that would have been idle mockery to a man who did not believe proves that this man had faith to be healed.

Two of them draw the conclusion about the day. Adam Clarke notes that Christ had asserted his Godhead a few verses earlier and here proves it, since nothing but omnipotence restores a withered hand in a moment; and he adds the neat point that because the cure came by a word without even a touch, the sabbath was unbroken even on the strictest reading of the letter of the law. Albert Barnes takes the two cases together as settling what may be done on the day, the cornfield a case of necessity and this one a case of mercy. John Gill and Charles Ellicott both borrow Mark’s detail that Jesus looked round on them with anger, grieved at the hardness of their hearts, and A.T. Robertson hopes the man stretched the hand out straight toward the watching Pharisees.
14:
The cure ends in a conspiracy. John Gill has them leave the synagogue filled with madness at arguments they could not answer and at a miracle that could only raise his standing with the people, and notes that they did not scruple to plot a death on the sabbath itself. Matthew Henry makes the pretext the point: they professed to be offended at sabbath-breaking, a capital crime under Exodus 35:2, when what galled them was a doctrine opposed to their pride and their worldly interest — it is no new thing to see the vilest practices cloaked with the most specious pretences, and they took counsel not to imprison or banish but to destroy him who came that we might have life. Albert Barnes and Charles Ellicott both fasten on Mark’s detail that the Herodians were drawn in: Barnes calls them a political party attached to Herod, ready to join any plot and still stung by the escape of the Babe of Bethlehem from Herod’s hands, and traces the whole to envy at a lost influence; Ellicott thinks these Pharisees included the delegation from Jerusalem, which raises the weight of the deliberation, and guesses the Herodians were already irritated by the contrast drawn at Matthew 11:8. A.T. Robertson marks the moment as the crisis of Pharisaic hatred, when they bolted out and conspired with rivals they despised, and observes that “destroy” here means kill. Adam Clarke reduces it to a single cause — nothing sooner leads to utter blindness and hardness of heart than envy. John Calvin finds it monstrous that the most distinguished teachers of the Law, entrusted with the government of the Church, should be engaged like robbers in contriving murder.

The withdrawal is read as deliberate rather than fearful. John Calvin insists the flight owed nothing to fear, since Christ was endued with the same fortitude of Spirit when he fled as when he later presented himself to die; it belongs to the self-emptying of Philippians 2:7, and he was in fact preserved by heavenly power rather than by concealment, since he took a great crowd with him and made the place famous by miracles — he withdrew for the sole purpose of not aggravating their rage. Jerome gives the same motive from their side, that he might remove from the Pharisees all opportunity of sin, and Hilary that he might be far from the counsels of the evil-hearted. Remigius offers the alternative that this was neither the time nor the place, since a prophet cannot perish out of Jerusalem (Luke 13:33), and notes the reversal that the multitude loved and followed the man the Pharisees agreed to destroy. Raban reads the “went out” as a mind gone alien from the Lord, taking counsel how to destroy life rather than how to find it, and draws the lesson that after doing something great we are not to seek praise abroad.

The catena attaches the Isaiah citation of Isaiah 42:1 here, and divides over the bruised reed. Jerome gives two readings: the man who will not hold out a hand to a sinner breaks a bruised reed and despises a spark of faith; or else the Jews are the bruised reed the Lord patiently endured, and the smoking flax the Gentiles, whose almost dead spark he raised into a flame. Hilary reverses the halves, taking the reed for the bruised bodies of the Gentiles reserved for salvation, and the smouldering flax for a Spirit not yet quite withdrawn from Israel. Augustine applies both to the persecutors, spared because he came not to judge them but to be judged by them. Chrysostom uses the prophecy differently again, as proof that one who is beloved and chosen does not break the law as an adversary of the Lawgiver.
15:
The retreat is described and then justified. John Gill takes the knowledge of the plot to be omniscience rather than report, and the departure to be timing rather than fear: his hour had not come and other work remained, so he wisely provided for his own safety. Albert Barnes calls it Christian prudence, since remaining would only have provoked them further, and fills in the scene from Mark: the withdrawal to the sea, the crowds pressing to the water’s edge, and the boat kept ready so he could address them apart from the press. Charles Ellicott notes that the coalition of the two parties drove him from Capernaum, so that in withdrawing he acted out the precept already given in Matthew 10:23. Adam Clarke makes it a rule for ministers: a man of God does not fear persecution, but leaves a place when the obstacles are humanly invincible and he cannot do good without occasioning much evil — yield to the stream when you cannot stem it — and rejection in one place has often established the gospel in another. On “he healed them all” John Gill, Adam Clarke and Charles Ellicott all read a limit into the words: all who needed healing and sought it.

The charge to silence is where they divide. John Gill thinks it was laid on the healed multitude and the unclean spirits alike, in a word that carries a threat, for mixed reasons: no desire for applause, no wish to provoke, no willingness yet to be taken. Albert Barnes keeps it simple: he desired concealment for now, to avoid the plots and save his life. Charles Ellicott notices that the command is general rather than fitted to one person, so the usual appeal to the spiritual discipline of the healed will not serve; the hour of conflict had not come, and he sought to work while it was day, wise as a serpent and harmless as a dove. Adam Clarke draws the opposite lesson, that Christ could have concealed himself as God but chose human means, to teach us not to neglect them in our necessity. John Lightfoot takes the sharpest line: it was neither a refusal to heal nor merely a shunning of applause, but a keeping of himself hidden from those who would not acknowledge him, on the principle of the parables of Matthew 13:13 — he would not be known by those who would not know him. John Calvin reads timing rather than concealment: he did not wish the report repressed, but allowed to strike root and bear fruit in season, since he was manifested gradually and by regular steps; and he rejected the confession extorted from the devils because he did not choose such witnesses.

On the citation itself, John Gill denies that Christ acted in order to fulfil it — the fulfilment is the evangelist’s observation, not the motive —. Albert Barnes makes it a correction of expectation: the disciples looked for a conqueror, and the prophecy describes one retiring and peaceful, strengthening the feeble instead of breaking them. Charles Ellicott is struck that so free a rendering, used of mere reticence, falls short of the prophecy’s full meaning, and concludes that power joined to such freedom from ostentation marks the true ideal King. A.T. Robertson, who elsewhere notes only that the participle means Jesus read thoughts already plain in their faces, calls the quotation a free reproduction of the Hebrew with side glances at the Septuagint, applying to Christ a prophecy others referred to Cyrus. John Calvin denies that the prediction was exhausted by the prohibition; it was one exhibition of a mildness running through the whole ministry, and its point is that the glory of Christ’s divinity is not less admirable for appearing under a veil of infirmity, unlike earthly kings who fill towns with commotion to draw admiration.
18:
The commentators divide over what “servant” concedes. John Gill hears the Father speaking to the church about Christ as mediator, a servant employed and obedient in the work of salvation, chosen from eternity and, in the Hebrew, upheld; the delight is not only in the only begotten Son but in the office and its discharge, declared aloud at the baptism and on the mount. Albert Barnes grounds the title in the humble condition and the form of a servant of Philippians 2:7. Adam Clarke makes it the answer to a deficit: God required a perfect service which sinful man could not render, and Jesus, taking man’s nature, performed the whole will of God and communicates grace to enable his followers. Charles Ellicott sets the verse in Isaiah’s larger portrait, where the servant of the Lord appears now as representing Israel’s righteousness, now its sins, now as prophet and messenger, now in solitary greatness or suffering — each aspect fulfilled highest in the Son of Man; the evangelist follows the Chaldee Paraphrase in referring the words to the Messiah, and the almost identical words heard at the baptism must have suggested the application. A.T. Robertson makes the same connection in a line, that “my beloved” recalls Matthew 3:17. John Calvin reads the opening “Behold” as God pointing with the finger to the person he is about to send, and insists that the servant is so called not as one of ordinary rank but by eminence, as the man called of God to the office (Hebrews 5:4); men measure Christ by their own sense only because they forget that redemption depends on grace alone, and so are not at liberty to reject him.

On “I will put my Spirit upon him,” Cyril of Jerusalem gathers the promise into a chain of texts — wisdom and understanding, counsel and might, knowledge and godliness — to show that the Spirit is one and undivided while his operations are various. The word rendered “judgment” draws a threefold answer. Albert Barnes and Adam Clarke both take the Hebrew behind it to mean law, precepts, a whole system or body of doctrine, and so the Christian scheme itself; Barnes finds the prophecy already fulfilled in the crowds from Idumea, beyond Jordan, and Tyre and Sidon at Mark 3:7. John Wesley notes that the Hebrew word signifies either mercy or justice, and takes it here for the merciful gospel published to the heathen. Charles Ellicott keeps the range wide enough to include a king’s work of teaching righteousness as well as executing it, and observes that Matthew, writing for Jews, records by anticipation the gentleness that had by then brought the Gentiles within reach of those life-giving judgments.

The refusal to strive is described the same way and explained differently. Albert Barnes hears a warrior who will not shout, retiring instead from the streets where crowds gathered, seeking no publicity. Adam Clarke makes it a test of discipleship — the spirit of Christ is not one of contention, murmuring, clamour or litigiousness, and whoever loves these does not belong to him. Charles Ellicott hears the pervading calmness that had impressed the evangelist, set against the wrangling of scribes, the violence of Roman officers, and the fury of leaders of revolt like Judas of Galilee, each of which Matthew had probably known. John Wesley reads the three clauses as a rising series, each expressing a higher degree of humility. John Gill alone makes it forensic: the Hebrew “he shall not cry” is the cry of a plaintiff, and Christ refused to bring any charge or accusation, leaving that to Moses, in whom they trusted. John Calvin turns it into a rebuke: it is an astonishing folly that men think less respectfully of Christ because he accommodates himself to their capacity, when appearing in glory he would simply swallow us up.
20:
John Gill opens by conceding that interpreters vary here, and what follows proves him right. John Lightfoot takes the figures as measures of noise rather than portraits of persons: they continue the description of the silent transaction of Christ’s own affairs, and mean he will make no more sound than the snap of a half-broken reed or the hiss of smoking flax doused with water — how different, he adds, from the Messiah the Jews expected, though they own the passage speaks of him. The others read persons. Albert Barnes takes the reed for feebleness and change, as at Matthew 11:7, standing for the poor and oppressed and for the contrite soul, and the smoking wick for the languishing graces of God’s people, which he feeds with oil until it blazes. Charles Ellicott reads the same way and makes the second figure a parable of souls whose light has grown dim, clogged by base desires and no longer fed with true oil, as in the lamps of Matthew 25:1; the self-righteous Pharisee gave thanks that his own lamp burned, while the Christ sought to trim the wick and pour in oil — and he suspects the publican-apostle had found the words fulfilled in his own experience. John Wesley is briefest: a convinced sinner bruised with the weight of sin, and one with the faintest spark of grace. Adam Clarke reports a further reading he does not adopt, that the figures mean the Jewish state, which Christ would not destroy but leave to expire of itself, since it already held the principles of its own destruction; he prefers the tender sense, that a bruised reed may recover under the influences of heaven and Jesus quenches no faint desire after salvation. A.T. Robertson stays with the words, noting the perfect passive participle, the curious augment copyists preserved where it does not belong, and images that picture Jesus in the strain of Matthew 11:28.

The closing clause divides them further. John Lightfoot notes that the Hebrew and the Septuagint read “unto truth,” and takes the victory to be the moment when Christ, having managed his affairs in humility, silence, poverty and patience — on earth and afterwards in his apostles — breaks forth at last as judge and conqueror against the nation that had made him and his suffer so. Albert Barnes makes judgment mean truth, the gospel, victorious though its conqueror is not the sort expected. Adam Clarke takes it for the gospel’s complete triumph over Jewish opposition and Gentile impiety alike. Charles Ellicott keeps the Hebrew reading in view: the tender compassion characterises the whole work of Christ until final judgment comes and truth prevails. John Calvin fastens on the word Matthew chose, which he calls very emphatic: the kingdom is not established without a great struggle, since the devil throws every possible difficulty in the way, and victory is had no other way than by fighting.

The Gentile clause is treated as a textual problem. John Gill observes that the preceding words are omitted, that Isaiah has “the isles shall wait for his law,” and that the word need not mean islands but mainland nations; the name is the gospel, which Isaiah calls his law, and the fulfilment had begun among the Idumeans, Tyrians and Sidonians then in attendance. Albert Barnes agrees that the isles denote Gentiles outside Judea, the idea unchanged. Charles Ellicott is blunter about the mechanism, that the Hebrew gives “in his law” and Matthew follows the Septuagint. John Calvin grants the change of words but holds the meaning identical: the grace of Christ will be shared by the Gentiles. Adam Clarke works from the Greek verb, which he renders “they shall hope”: to hope in that name is to expect all things from him alone, to despise earthly promises by comparison, and to bear this life’s losses in prospect of a purchased felicity.
22:
The Gloss explains why the miracle is narrated at all: the charge that follows was worse than the sabbath charge, referring a work of divine power to an unclean spirit; so the evangelist sets down first the deed that occasioned it. John Gill puts it shortly after the return from the sea, in a house, the man brought by others out of compassion and confidence in what Christ had lately done. Charles Ellicott warns that the passage is a stumbling-block for harmonists, since Luke places it much later and Mark just after the mission of the Twelve; Mark also has the Pharisees who brought the charge coming down from Jerusalem, as those emissaries elsewhere do.

Whether this repeats Matthew 9:32 is disputed. John Gill says the two are alike in effect, in the cavil and in the answer, and yet not the same case, since that man was only dumb. Charles Ellicott agrees, the earlier man being simply dumb while here the suspension of sense and will is more complicated, and thinks the charge was repeated as occasion arose and answered in like words. Augustine handles the other half: Luke 11:14 calls the man dumb only and places the incident elsewhere, but silence on one particular is no reason to suppose a different man, since the rest agrees exactly.

The cause is disputed too. John Calvin observes that many are blind or deaf by natural defect, but this man had no fault in the nerves that conduct vision nor in the proportion of his tongue; nor need we wonder at such liberty against the bodily senses, when God justly permits Satan to pervert the faculties of the soul. John Wesley presses it into a question: many supposed the defects merely natural, but the Spirit gives the true account — how many disorders now taken for natural may have the same cause? Chrysostom reads strategy: the demon had blocked both inlets of belief, hearing and sight, and Christ opened both.

Most then turn the cure into a figure, and the figures differ. Jerome counts three miracles in one person at one moment, fulfilled daily in conversion: the demon cast out when the light of faith is first seen, the stopped mouth opened to praise. Augustine states it flatly: he who does not believe is truly demoniac, blind and dumb, and whoever neither understands the faith nor confesses is subject to the devil. Matthew Henry works it out in detail: a soul led captive is blind in the things of God and dumb at the throne of grace, for Satan blinds the eye of faith and seals up the lips of prayer; when his power breaks, the eyes open to God’s glory and the lips to his praise. Adam Clarke divides the captivity three ways: the heart filled with love of sin, the eyes blinded to guilt and judgment, the tongue hindered from prayer but loosed for blasphemy and slander. Hilary alone reads the man historically rather than morally: after the withered hand was healed in the synagogue, the salvation of the Gentiles had to be figured in another afflicted man, one who had housed a demon and was now made fit to receive God and praise the works of Christ.

On the name flung at Christ, Remigius supplies a long etymology, tracing Beel and Baal and Beelphegor, and deriving the second half from a servant made priest of a temple of Baal and set to drive off the flies drawn by the victims’ blood; the name means the man of flies; having nothing meaner to throw at the Lord, they called him prince of the demons. Raban notes that the god belonged to Ekron, and draws the contrast running through the chapter: the unlearned multitude always wondered at the Lord’s works, while the Pharisees denied what was done or perverted by ill interpretation what they could not deny.
23:
The crowd’s reaction is agreed on and its force disputed. John Gill limits the amazement to the greater part of the common people, and finds in them not admiration only but conviction, faith and confession. Albert Barnes supplies the reasoning: they knew Isaiah 35:5, where the eyes of the blind are opened, and inferred the promised Messiah — an inference drawn by plain men and not by the Pharisees, which prompts his remark that men of common sense often see the meaning of the Bible while those filled with a science falsely so called are blinded. Adam Clarke reads the question as an assertion, that the miracles sufficiently prove him the true Messiah. Charles Ellicott notes only that the crowd reaches for the most popular of all the titles of the Christ, as the blind man had at Matthew 9:27. Against these, A.T. Robertson points out that the Greek form of the question expects the answer “no,” put that way because of the hostility in the air, and that the imperfect tense has the crowds standing outside themselves with excitement. John Calvin reaches nearly the same conclusion from the sense rather than the syntax: some take it for a full affirmation, but the words convey no such thing — the crowd was struck by an unexpected occurrence and got only as far as the thought that he might be the Christ, which is still no small proficiency.

The counter-charge is credited to a different set of opponents. John Gill thinks these were probably not the Pharisees who had gone out to plot, but others come down from Judea and Jerusalem who had seen the miracle, moved to speak by how ready the people were to own Jesus as Messiah. Albert Barnes sets out the necessity they were under: a manifest miracle had been done, the common people were drawing the proper inference, their own authority was declining, and any account they gave had to concede superhuman power, since no one could deny it — so the charge had two objects at once, to grant that a work above man had occurred and to throw all possible contempt on the worker. Charles Ellicott makes the same point as an admission: that the Pharisees were driven to assume demoniacal agency shows they accepted the reality of the healing they had watched; and he judges from the wording that the charge was whispered among the people rather than addressed to Jesus. A.T. Robertson calls it desperation, forced on them by an excited crowd and a fact they could not deny. John Calvin puts it hardest: unable to withhold acknowledgement of something so open and manifest, they did not merely obscure the praise of the miracle but tried to turn it into a reproach, as though it were done by magical enchantment.

On the name itself the accounts diverge. Albert Barnes derives it as the god of flies, or of filth, and so of idolatry, an opprobrious name given to the vilest of the devils. John Lightfoot approaches it from the other end, through the rabbinic duty of reproaching idols with odious names: it was held almost a matter of religion, so that what the nations called the face of God the Jews were to call the face of a dog, and the town once called Beth-el was afterwards called Beth-aven; all jeering was forbidden except the jeering of idolatry. On that footing he takes the common ignominious element in the name to be Zebul, meaning dung or a dunghill, an idol-temple being spoken of as a dunghill — a derivation quite distinct from the flies.
25:
That the answer is made to a thought rather than a word is what they notice first. John Wesley observes simply that as yet they had said it only in their hearts. Chrysostom explains why: the accusation was so unreasonable, and they so feared the multitude, that they did not dare publish it. He adds that Christ, having let the earlier charge pass so that further miracles might teach them, now rebukes them because they persist, yet does not repeat their thoughts back to them, his object being to do the sinners good and not to proclaim their sin. Jerome makes the point evidential: by answering the thought and not the word, he compelled them to reckon with one who sees the heart’s secrets. John Gill and Adam Clarke both take that knowledge for a proof of omniscience, and Gill draws the conclusion openly, that it proves his deity and so his Messiahship. Albert Barnes reaches it by way of Scripture, since to know the thoughts of the heart belongs to God alone (Psalm 139:2, Jeremiah 17:10). John Lightfoot supplies the Jewish form of the test and turns it on the accusers: it was written of the Messiah that he should smell and judge, discerning the man without the sight of the eyes (Isaiah 11:3); when Ben Cozba claimed the title, the rabbis put him to that trial and killed him when he failed. John Calvin uses it to explain the severity of the rebuke: many judge wrongly through ignorance and rashness rather than concealed venom, and Christ dealt harder with these because he was witness of an inward malice. Charles Ellicott adds that of all the charges this caused the greatest pain and drew the most indignant answer, his healing work being represented as the Tempter’s bait.

The argument is read as a dilemma, and only one of them doubts it. The Gloss states it cleanly: he casts out demons either by the power of God or by the prince of demons; if the former, the accusation is malicious; if the latter, that kingdom is divided and cannot stand. Albert Barnes makes the case from their own premises: it is their doctrine that Satan possessed these men and theirs that he helped cast him out, so on their account he has helped undo his own work and shows less than human prudence. Adam Clarke puts it as a question any ruler would answer: Satan, like every other potentate, must wish to rule his empire in peace, so how should he league with one who is destroying his kingdom? Charles Ellicott notes what the reply assumes: a kingdom of evil, compact and organised with a distinct unity of purpose, to which the laws of other kingdoms apply. Jerome presses the further difficulty, that if the demons withdraw at their prince’s command to work a concerted fraud, that still leaves the cures of bodily diseases unaccounted for. A.T. Robertson catalogues the means rather than the matter: conditions, sarcasm, rhetorical question and merciless logic, laying the insincerity bare. John Calvin alone registers a reservation: the refutation may appear not quite satisfactory, since Satan does sometimes present an appearance of discord in order to entrap men by superstitions.

Hilary leaves the plain sense to others and reads the three terms as history. The Law was from God, and by the Law came the promise of the kingdom to Israel; a kingdom of the Law divided against itself must be destroyed, and Israel lost the Law when the nation whose the Law was rejected its fulfilment. The city is Jerusalem, whose destruction is here declared, since it raged against the Lord and drove out the apostles with the multitude who believed. He adds the point that whoever made the division in Satan’s house must be granted a higher power than those divided by it.
26:
John Gill reads the second horn as Satan casting out the rest of the devils of whom he is prince, and Charles Ellicott corrects that from the Greek: the name has the article in both places, so it is not one Satan casting out another but the one great adversary casting out himself. He adds that Satan is not personally identified with the deaf or dumb spirit, but that where evil enters a soul he enters with it, so that there is a kind of ubiquity in the power of evil answering to that of good. Adam Clarke puts the reply in Christ’s mouth: were I on Satan’s side I would confirm his influence among you, whereas I oppose his maxims by my doctrine and his influence by my power. John Wesley reduces it to a question: does not that subtle spirit know this is no way to establish his kingdom?

“Your children” is the disputed phrase, and the readings run three ways. John Lightfoot, Albert Barnes, Adam Clarke and Charles Ellicott all take them for disciples of the Pharisees who practised exorcism, like those of Acts 19:13. John Calvin reaches the same identification by elimination, rejecting the children of the nation, the apostles and the ancient prophets alike, since a reference to the dead is forced where the comparison is plainly of the present. Jerome allows either the Jewish exorcists or the apostles, who are of that race, and prefers the apostles, who will judge from twelve thrones; on the first reading the judgment is by comparison rather than authority, since the Pharisees credited the same work to God in their own and to the prince of demons in Christ. Hilary takes the apostles too: if they work by Christ and Christ by the Spirit of God, the kingdom is already transferred to them through the office of the Mediator. Chrysostom notices the wording rather than the referent: he said not “my disciples” but “your children,” leaving a door open for return and no impudent excuse for ingratitude, since the same works in the apostles drew no such charge — never the actions but the person was opposed. Raban adds only that the apostles knew in conscience they had learnt no evil art of him.

Whether those exorcists actually cast out demons is disputed too. Albert Barnes holds that the words prove no such power, only the claim, the practice being magic or jugglery. John Lightfoot is harsher: what they did was less a casting out than a delusion of the people, Satan seeming expelled by compact with himself in order to deceive the better. Charles Ellicott takes the opposite view on logical grounds, that the question is valid only if the children really did cast out demons and not by Beelzebub; nor need we assume mere pretence, since earnestness, prayer, fasting and faith intensify the power of will before which a frenzied soul yields. John Wesley agrees that some of them really did it, though the sons of Sceva could not. Adam Clarke and John Calvin leave the fact aside and press the inequality: the Pharisees must give up the argument or admit themselves leagued with the devil, and their unequal verdicts show a motive of blind love or hatred, envy condemning in one what it applauds in another.

On the conclusion, the Gloss is briefest: the weakening of the devil’s kingdom is the increase of God’s. Augustine presses it from their own premise, that on their account the kingdom has come — the kingdom in which the wicked are condemned and separated from the faithful now doing penance. Jerome counts three senses of the kingdom here: Christ himself, unrecognised in the midst (Luke 17:21); the kingdom preached as at hand (Matthew 3:2); and the kingdom to be taken from the Jews and given to a nation bringing forth its fruit.
28:
The alternative closed, the conclusion follows. John Gill notes that all three persons had a hand in the miracle, done by Christ, in the Father’s name, by the power of the Spirit. Albert Barnes equates the Spirit with the power of God, citing Luke’s “finger of God” and the magicians at Exodus 8:19; the two reigns stand opposed, so if God expels the one the other has come. Charles Ellicott traces the figure further, to the hand of the Lord strong upon the prophet in Ezekiel 3:14 and the tables written with the finger of God in Exodus 31:18, then formulates the argument: the work was confessedly superhuman, so from Satan or from God; the first is excluded by what precedes; therefore the worker is what he claimed, and the kingdom had burst on men unawares. Adam Clarke suspects the Spirit is named in contrast with the magical incantations of the Jews, who professed to expel demons by fumigations and washings, and stresses the verb, which means to arrive suddenly; they pretended to expect the kingdom, but being unready for its proofs showed themselves too carnal to mind spiritual things. John Calvin makes the same word the sting: without any request of theirs God appears as their Redeemer, and they do all in their power to drive him away. Christ has stopped defending himself and treats them as convicted men, refusing to rest in one miracle and turning to the object of his whole coming.

The third answer is a parable, and its terms are read variously. Charles Ellicott assigns them from the fuller version at Luke 11:21: the strong man is Satan, the house the region subject to him, the goods the demons by which he holds it, the binding the check given by freeing the possessed, the spoiling the final victory. Jerome makes the house this world, set in evil not by the majesty of the Creator but by the greatness of the sinner. Augustine makes the goods all the unbelievers, and the binding the removal of every power to hinder the faithful from following Christ. Adam Clarke brings it inside a man: through sin we become the very dwelling place of Satan, having surrendered of our own accord, since whoever gives up his soul to sin gives it to the devil. Raban reads the spoiling twice over: the setting free of those Christ foresaw would be his own and their joining to the Church, and the dividing of the whole world among the apostles and their successors for conversion. Albert Barnes keeps to the logic, that a house cannot be broken into unless its owner is first rendered helpless, so the taking of the goods proves the binding; and “spoil” here keeps its older sense of plundering by violence.

What the word “strong” concedes is the last question. Chrysostom takes it for the adversary’s old reign, arisen out of our own sloth, and observes that Christ says not rob but spoil, showing it done with power; the saying is also a prophecy, since Christ will take all error out of the world and dissolve the craft of the devil. Jerome draws the warning: the strong man is bound and bruised under the Lord’s foot, yet we ought not be careless, for the conqueror himself has pronounced our adversary strong. John Calvin explains why superior force was needed: the tyranny is defended on every side, and men are so firmly bound that they cherish their slavery. John Wesley states the sequence plainly, that Christ, coming into what was then eminently Satan’s house, first bound him and then took his spoils. Cyril of Jerusalem puts the verse to a use none of the others do, against those who assign the soul to one God and the body to another: he who casts both into hell must first have bound the strong man and spoiled his goods.
30:
The fourth answer is a maxim, and the first question is who it is about. John Gill refers it chiefly to Satan, since the enmity between the serpent and the seed of the woman is original and implacable, an open war between parties with different interests and different methods, so that neither could lend the other assistance. Jerome argues it from the context in the same direction and lists the oppositions: the one seeks to hold souls captive and the Lord to set them free, the one preaches idols and the Lord the knowledge of the true God, the one draws men to sin and the Lord calls them back to virtue — and he adds the caution that although the words may be applied to heretics and schismatics besides, they are not spoken of them here. Chrysostom hears the Jews included, classed with the devil because they were against Christ and scattered what he would gather, though he allows it fair to take the saying of Christ himself. John Calvin reports two readings and chooses the second: either an argument from contraries, that Christ cannot reign until the devil is overthrown, or — his own preference — a charge that the scribes are doubly opposed to the kingdom, since even a failure to assist counts as opposition, and theirs is a furious and avowed one. He extends it further than the occasion, holding that those who do not employ all the means in their power are unworthy to be reckoned of Christ’s flock, because indolence retards the work.

The others generalise it at once. Albert Barnes makes it a principle that there can be but two parties in the universe, and reads the second clause from the harvest: whoever does not gather with the reaper scatters. Adam Clarke prefers a shepherd behind the image — he who will not help the true shepherd gather the flock into the fold most likely wishes to scatter it, that he may steal and destroy — and he adds a small scholarly note, that although the saying looks proverbial he could find no parallel to it among the rabbins, or in the Greek or Roman writers. Clarke also presses the application: when Christ, his truth and his servants are assaulted, whoever does not espouse their cause incurs the guilt of deserting him, and many who flatter themselves that they work with him are in fact scattering. John Wesley says the same in a line, that there are no neuters in this war and none on earth who neither promote nor obstruct the kingdom. A.T. Robertson draws the line of cleavage between Christ and his enemies then and now, and finds the choice unavoidable: we gather with him or scatter to the four winds, Satan being the arch-waster and Christ the collector. Hilary keeps it tied to the charge in hand, that the saying shows how far Christ is from having borrowed any power from the devil, and warns how great the danger of thinking amiss of him, since not to be with him is the same as to be against him.

The maxim appears to contradict another, and two of them address it. Chrysostom distinguishes the subjects: at Luke 9:50 the saying that whoever is not against you is for you concerns a man who was on their side, while here the subject is the devil, our adversary, so the two are not contrary. Charles Ellicott reaches the same result by treating them as opposite poles of one truth: in the struggle between light and darkness there is no neutrality, and the man the disciples complained of was fighting the devil in Christ’s name and therefore with him, while the Pharisees were hindering and slandering that same work and therefore against him, gathering nothing of God’s harvest and so scattering it.
31:
Most of the moderns answer narrowly. John Gill ties the saying to the occasion, the imputing to diabolical assistance of what was done by the Spirit, and holds that they knew better. Albert Barnes defines it as charging Jesus with working miracles by the prince of devils, and takes Mark 3:30, “because they said he had an unclean spirit,” to fix the sense; to call God’s highest mercy the devil’s work argues the deepest depravity. Adam Clarke and John Wesley agree exactly, Wesley remarking that after all the volumes written on it nothing in the Bible is plainer. A.T. Robertson holds that these Pharisees had already committed it, and that some still do who ridicule the manifest work of God’s Spirit and assign it to the devil. Against that, Charles Ellicott notes that the best manuscripts read simply “against the Spirit,” and declines to say the Pharisees had committed the sin, only that they drifted toward it: to watch a man delivered from Satan and call the work evil is to be out of sympathy with goodness itself, leaving no opening for repentance and so none for pardon. John Calvin clears away a rival definition, that the sin is obstinacy persisted in till death; Christ would have spoken to no purpose, and the term cannot be stretched over every sort of crime.

Why the blasphemy is graver than a word against the Son of Man divides them. Jerome makes the difference the flesh: to stumble at the body and think him no more than man finds pardon because of the body’s little worth, whereas to perceive the works of God plainly, be unable to deny them, and still speak falsely of them out of jealousy is not forgiven. Chrysostom puts it the other way: grant they stumbled at the flesh, but of the Spirit they had knowledge enough, since the prophets spoke by him, and can plead no ignorance. Hilary makes it the denial itself: nothing is so beyond pardon as to deny in Christ what is of God and to take away the substance of the Father’s Spirit in him. Augustine rules out the wrong reason, that the Spirit is greater in the Trinity than the Son, which no heretic ever affirmed, and harmonises the wording with Luke 12:10. John Calvin denies it on his own ground, that the whole fulness of the Godhead dwells in Christ (Colossians 2:9), so a greater majesty in the Spirit cannot be the reason.

Three Latin voices use the verse against a named error. Remigius observes that sins are forgiven not universally but to those who have done due penitence, overthrowing the Novatianist claim that the lapsed could not rise again. The Gloss takes the last clause to destroy the old Alexandrian opinion that after many ages all sinners obtain pardon. Gregory argues the opposite way from the same clause: since what is denied of one sin must be admitted of others, some are remitted in the world to come — idle discourse, immoderate laughter, anxious care in worldly affairs — though none is purged there who has not merited it here. Chrysostom reads the threat as warning rather than doctrine of the hereafter, distinguishing those punished in this life only, those punished in the next only, and these who suffer both, as the Jews did at the taking of Jerusalem.

Two turn to the anxious. Adam Clarke writes for those troubled by the fear that they have committed this sin, and answers that no one who believes the divine mission of Jesus Christ can have done so. Matthew Henry observes the same inversion, that humble believers are tempted to think it of themselves while those nearest to it seldom fear it, and reasons that repentance and faith are gifts God would not give one he meant never to pardon, so the trembling sinner has the witness in himself.
32:
The lighter half of the contrast is taken up first. John Gill insists that the Son of Man here is Christ and not man in general, the title marking the meanness and obscurity of the human nature in which he appeared; and he lists what ignorance might say — denying him the Messiah, reproaching his parentage and his education, objecting to his company with publicans and sinners — all of which may afterwards be repented of and pardoned, as they were in Saul the Pharisee, who is his standing instance of a forgiven blasphemer.

The disputed words are the last ones, and each commentator locates the two ages differently. John Wesley takes the phrase as a Jewish proverb for a thing that will never be done, adding that it means besides that the punishment will not be escaped here or hereafter. Adam Clarke is satisfied that it means neither under this dispensation, the Jewish, nor under that which is to come, the Christian, since the age to come is a constant phrase for the times of the Messiah in the Jewish writers; he ranks the sin with the presumptuous sins of Numbers 15:30, for which the Law provided no forgiveness, and suggests that the punishment is the destruction of the body while mercy might still reach the soul. Charles Ellicott divides the ages at the same point but reads the consequence differently: for the original hearers this age was the time before the Christ and the age to come what should follow, so that Christ stood on the boundary line of the two; since the change proved to be slow and continuous growth rather than a sudden new order, we still think of ourselves as living in this age and place the next beyond the grave. John Calvin refuses any intermediate period altogether: the meaning is that those who have blasphemed against the Spirit have no reason to expect pardon in this life or acquittal at the last judgment, and it is a torturing of the expression to find a middle state in it when the second clause plainly denotes the final judgment.

Whether the verse implies remission after death is therefore the real question. John Lightfoot answers that those who argue so have not seen what Christ had in view, and sets out the rabbinic scale he takes the phrase from: he who transgresses an affirmative precept and repents at once is pardoned; he who transgresses a negative precept has judgment suspended by repentance and expiated on the day of atonement; he who has incurred cutting off or death by the Sanhedrin has judgment suspended by repentance and the day of atonement while the strokes laid on him wipe off the sin; but for the man who profanes the Name, neither repentance nor the day of atonement nor scourges can wipe it off — all merely suspend, and death wipes it off. On that footing the saying belongs to a known Jewish gradation of expiations, not to a doctrine of pardon in the world to come. John Calvin presses the same conclusion against the schoolmen by their own rule: they hold that guilt is freely pardoned while punishment and satisfaction remain to be exacted, which concedes that no one whose guilt is unpardoned before death has any hope of salvation — and guilt, not punishment, is what this discourse is about. Charles Ellicott alone reads the clause the other way, taking the words to imply that some sins do wait for their full forgiveness, the entire cancelling of the past, until the age that will witness the final Advent.
33:
Whether the saying is a command or a test divides them at once. Augustine splits it: “make the tree good” is a precept of health, while “make the tree corrupt” is no command but a warning to men who thought that being evil they could still speak good things — the man must be changed first, that his works may be changed, and Christ found us all corrupt trees but gave power to become sons of God. Charles Ellicott notes that the proverb would be a call to consistency if addressed to half-hearted men, but these were not neutral; so “make” means reckon, and what is asked is logical rather than practical consistency — if casting out demons is good, the power it flows from is good. John Calvin heads off the same misreading, warning that some foolishly infer that every man can regulate his own life, when the wording is rhetorical; it is aimed at a pretended sanctity so imposing that nobody dared name the Pharisees’ vices, and Christ removes the mask by declaring nothing more inconsistent with honesty than hypocrisy. Chrysostom makes it a rule of evidence they have broken: though the tree causes the fruit, the fruit is the evidence of the tree, and they, having no fault to allege against the works, sentence the tree instead. Jerome names the form, the unavoidable syllogism that shuts a man in on both sides: if the devil is evil he cannot do good works, so if the works are good the devil did not do them.

The rest apply it. John Gill puts the demand plainly, that they must call both good or both bad. Albert Barnes turns it into a test that cuts both ways: if his works are the devil’s he is corrupt, and if not the charge is blasphemy — and their own works may be tried by the same rule. Adam Clarke reads it of the heart: the works resemble it, and nothing good can come from a corrupt one until it is renewed by the Spirit of God. Matthew Henry makes the figure a fountain instead: the heart is the spring and words the streams, and only the salt of grace cast in will heal the waters. John Wesley turns it back on the accusers as a claim, that they may know him by his fruits, by his converting of sinners to God. Hilary alone looks past the occasion: to hold oneself neuter, worshipping Christ as God while denying him a common substance with the Father, is itself blasphemy against the Spirit.

On the reproach, John Gill answers their boast of Abraham’s seed by pointing to their immediate ancestry, and Charles Ellicott presses the figure home: nothing but the serpent’s hiss could come from a brood of vipers. Albert Barnes pauses over the severity, granting that these are strong expressions for the meek and lowly Jesus but denying they came of anger, being a just declaration of character. A.T. Robertson observes that the Baptist used the same words at Matthew 3:7, but these men had deliberately taken Satan’s side, the heart spurting out good or evil according to the supply within. Adam Clarke works the image forward: wicked words are the overflowings of a heart more than full of wickedness, holy words of one filled with the Spirit. John Calvin explains why speech alone is pressed: their falsehood betrayed a malice less visible in the rest of their life, and hypocrisy that colours sin calls for more terrible thunder than other sins. Raban reads the reproach as naming them imitators of the devil for wilfully speaking against good works, and puts the treasure in the intention of the thoughts, by which the Judge weighs the deed — a great outward work from a cold heart earning little. John Wesley states the rule in a line: the heart is known by the conversation.
35:
John Gill takes the good man for a regenerated man and the good treasure for nothing native to him but the grace received out of Christ’s fulness, a treasure because it collects riches each more precious than gold. Charles Ellicott finds a whole parable folded into the word: every thought is added to an accumulating store within and passes out into word or deed; and though most characters look mixed, where the unity of loving God is absent the distraction of loving self makes the store predominantly evil. Adam Clarke adds that “of the heart” is missing from upwards of a hundred manuscripts and most ancient versions, and looks to be a copyist’s explanation; the good heart is itself the treasury, its treasure the love of God and of all mankind.

What counts as an idle word is disputed, and the range of answers is wide. Chrysostom restricts it to a word that accuses falsely, though some extend it to all light talk; he notices the tact of the wording, that Christ said not “which ye have spoken” but framed it for the whole race, and that on this rule the accusers have everything to fear, since a man is judged by what he said and not by what is said of him. Jerome defines it as a word that does not edify, but keeps a harder class beyond it: whoever deals in buffoon jests is guilty not of an idle word but of a sinful one. Gregory makes it one lacking rightness in itself or a reason of just necessity. Albert Barnes and Adam Clarke grant that it literally means useless but hold the context requires more, Clarke noting that the Hebrew behind it covers what is wicked and injurious, and that a few manuscripts substituted “evil” outright. Charles Ellicott resists that narrowing: Christ says not every evil word but every useless one, since random utterances betray character more than deliberate speech; nor is a man condemned for each, only held to account, as it enters the total by which he is estimated. A.T. Robertson agrees that it means ineffective, and adds that judgment here is by words as elsewhere by deeds, both real tests of character. John Calvin reads it as an argument from less to greater, answering those who find it too severe by the purpose for which tongues were made and the time we are told to redeem (Ephesians 5:16); yet since no one keeps such a watch, rigour would leave us in despair, so he rests our hope on God burying our sins in forgetfulness (Psalm 143:2). John Wesley keeps the widest sense, every discourse not conducive to the glory of God.

The closing sentence raises the question of justification. John Gill notes that although it has been treated as a quotation, no such scripture exists; it is a proverb, or a reference to courts proceeding on a man’s own confession, and John Calvin agrees it was often in the people’s mouths. Charles Ellicott strips the term of later controversy: justified here means acquitted, the opposite of condemned, so men are justified by faith, by works and by words alike — faith as the root of character, words as its most spontaneous manifestation, works as its more permanent result. John Calvin guards the same ground from the other side, calling it childish to set this against the righteousness of faith, since upright speech grounds nothing but keeps a man from his own tongue’s condemnation. Remigius adds that no one is justified for good words unless they come from the inmost heart and an entire purpose. Albert Barnes holds that words are a chief part of what condemns but not the whole, John Wesley that they are produced in evidence with tempers and works. Adam Clarke ends where the practical weight lies: many count words for nothing when eternity depends on them.
38:
The tone of the request is what most notice first. John Gill takes these for a different set of Pharisees from those who charged him with Beelzebub, and reads the address as flattery: not Samaritan or magician now, but teacher, allowed the title while the office of prophet is withheld until he performs. Chrysostom sees the same shift and draws a conclusion from the reply: when they railed he answered mildly, and now that they come with smooth words he rebukes them sharply, being above either affection, neither angered by evil speaking nor won by flattery. Matthew Henry makes the courtesy the warning, that all are not Christ’s servants who call him Master, and grants what was reasonable in the demand: a man taking down a religion established by miracles should produce the like credentials (Exodus 4:8), though it was unreasonable to ask now, after so many signs — proud men prescribe to God and then plead the refusal as an excuse. Adam Clarke puts it as a rule, that pride, vain curiosity and incredulity never have proof sufficient; John Wesley supplies the unspoken condition, that otherwise they will not believe; and A.T. Robertson registers astonishment at men who had just accused him of league with Satan and could then blandly ask a sign, as if the other miracles were not signs.

What sign they wanted is answered differently. Albert Barnes lays the weight on “from heaven”: they may not have doubted the miracles, only found them short of decisive, and wanted something beyond dispute — a comet, thunder, a sudden darkness, food rained down. Jerome guesses at precedents, fire from heaven as in Elijah’s case or thunder and rain out of season as in Samuel’s, and turns the request round: if a man cavils at what he sees, handles and profits by, what will he make of things that come down from heaven? He even raises the objection against himself, that the magicians in Egypt also produced signs from the sky. Charles Ellicott keeps it simpler, reading the demand as a challenge to the authority with which Christ had spoken as judge of all men. Raban answers by pointing out what was actually granted: a sign not from heaven, which they were unworthy to see, but from the deep beneath, while the heavenly sign was reserved for the disciples, in figure on the mount and in truth at the ascension. He adds that the name Jonah, the dove or the mourner, fits the one on whom the Spirit descended as a dove and who bore our sorrows, and that the fish shows forth the death Christ suffered — the one cast up on dry land, the other risen in glory. He draws the warning too, that the Jews stood as guilty as the Ninevites and would be destroyed unless they repented, though like them they need not despair of pardon if they repented after the resurrection.

Two of the fathers begin the reckoning of the three days that occupies the next verse. Augustine disposes of an ingenious attempt to make the hours fit, counting the three hours of darkness at the crucifixion as a night and the three restored hours as a day; even so the sum reaches only two days and two nights, so the explanation lies in the scriptural habit of putting a part for the whole. Jerome states the same conclusion without argument: not three whole days and nights, but part of the preparation day, the whole sabbath, and part of the Lord’s day. Chrysostom reads the refusal as threat rather than denial, since a sign was given them when they learned his power by their own punishment and saw their city thrown down; and the resurrection needed the figure to go before it, since the cross itself would not have been believed without signs to testify to it.
39:
The reproach is explained from the prophets. Albert Barnes, Charles Ellicott and A.T. Robertson all take the marriage figure for the key, Israel the wife and apostasy the adultery, so that this generation has broken the tie binding it to its Lord and asks a sign instead of resting in the proofs already given. John Wesley widens it: all who love the world and seek its friendship are adulterers on that definition. Adam Clarke and Albert Barnes add that the charge was literal as well, Clarke citing the abolition of the trial by the bitter waters in that period because so many were found guilty; Clarke urges two renderings besides, that generation here means a race of people, and that the verb means seeking another sign after so many. John Lightfoot supplies the Jewish side: their own schools held that signs were not to be looked for except from a fit generation, the voice at Jericho and again at Jabneh saying a man was present worthy for the Spirit to rest on, but the generation was not. John Calvin reads the epithet as illegitimacy, a race degenerated from the holy fathers, then raises the difficulty nobody else does: God was not angry when Gideon asked a sign and then a second, gave one to Hezekiah unsolicited, and blamed Ahaz for refusing to ask — so the offence cannot lie in the asking. Charles Ellicott raises a smaller difficulty, that the refusal seems to put the healings outside the class of signs when Christ had referred the Baptist’s messengers to those very works at Matthew 11:5; the context settles it, only one sign of the kind demanded being given.

The fish is a question of natural history to two of them. John Gill denies that Scripture says a whale at all, objecting that the swallow is too small and there are none in that sea; he suggests a large sea dog in whose belly whole men have been found in their armour. Albert Barnes reaches the same conclusion independently: a shark is likelier, and the Greek word need mean no more than a large fish.

The reckoning of the three days is the standing problem. Adam Clarke and John Wesley appeal to the eastern habit of counting any part of a day as the whole, with the fast of Esther 4:16 followed by the third day as the parallel; Wesley adds that the Hebrews, having no single word for a natural day, said night and day for it. Albert Barnes argues from silence: the Jews knew the prophecy and would have seized on it to convict him of falsehood had the reckoning been irregular, and no such charge was ever made.
