John Lightfoot reaches it through a rabbinic parallel, the thirty-six hours assigned to the standing of the sun at Joshua’s prayer, and notes that the hours from the giving up of the ghost to the resurrection come to nearly the same, so the phrase agrees with their own computation. A.T. Robertson is briefest: popular speech for three days and no more, since Jesus rose on the third day and not the fourth.

What the sign consists in is disputed too. Charles Ellicott reports the critical view that Matthew’s explanation was an addition and the sign fulfilled simply by preaching repentance, and rejects it: the preaching was no sign at all, only the fish and the gourd have that character, and the gourd is out of the question. Albert Barnes locates it in the deliverance: as the Ninevites believed Jonah on the strength of his preservation, so the resurrection is the evidence offered here. Cyril of Jerusalem answers those who demand proof that a man three days dead can rise by pressing the resemblance: both were sent to preach repentance, though the one fled and the other came willingly, and both slept while the sea rose about the ship.
41:
The two comparisons are graded. Chrysostom calls the second the greater, since Jonah went to Nineveh while the queen did not wait for Solomon to come to her: a woman, a foreigner, living at that distance, unafraid of death in her wish to hear wise words — and he sets the contrast in Christ’s mouth: she rose from the ends of the earth while he goes round their towns and villages, and Solomon spoke of trees and timber while he speaks of unspeakable mysteries. Jerome grades the first the same way: Jonah preached three days and Christ for years, Jonah to an unbelieving foreign nation and Christ to God’s own people, Jonah with his voice alone while Christ, working so many wonders, is charged with Beelzebub — and he takes “here” as an adverb of place, not a pronoun. Adam Clarke makes a fourfold version of the list, adds that the term is neuter and means something more rather than someone greater, and presses the moral: a whole people repented who had neither Moses nor the prophets and perhaps no preacher but that one. Charles Ellicott compares the reasoning about Tyre and Sidon at Matthew 11:21, marking the difference that there the appeal was to what might have been and here to what happened; and he observes that no chapter holds bolder assertions of superhuman majesty — greater than the temple, than Jonah, than Solomon — claims no mere man could rightly make. John Calvin keeps the contrast on the audiences: men who had never heard a word of the true God repented at the voice of an unknown foreigner, while the country that was the sanctuary of heavenly doctrine would not hear the Son of God; and if that nation stood convicted for despising Christ on earth, we are worse than any unbelievers if we despise him now that he speaks from heaven. A.T. Robertson puts the warning as forecast: they will disbelieve to the end and put him to death, and he will rise again, a sign for their confusion if not their conversion.

What the condemning amounts to is a second question. Jerome denies it is a sentence at all, making it the comparison of their example. John Gill allows two senses, the rising of witnesses to testify in court or the general resurrection, and Charles Ellicott settles on the first, that the word means standing up as a witness. Remigius reads it the other way and gets doctrine from it: one resurrection of good and bad is implied, against those who taught two, and judgment follows straight upon it, against the opinion that a thousand years divide them. Albert Barnes fills in the city’s history instead, its walls and towers, the destruction suspended two hundred years by the repentance and executed when the Tigris flooded and threw down part of the wall, exactly as foretold.

Her country divides them. John Gill places Sheba in southern Arabia and collects the names she goes by, ending with the historian who calls her queen of Egypt and Ethiopia. Albert Barnes and Adam Clarke take her for a queen of Arabia south of Judea, and read “the uttermost parts of the earth” as an idiom for great distance; John Wesley keeps it literal in a limited way, that this was the furthest land in that direction, being bounded by the sea. John Calvin dissents and follows the historians in making her queen of Ethiopia, with Meroe on the Nile for capital, since the Sheba of the genealogies lay eastward. Charles Ellicott adds a point of Greek, that it is a queen of the south and men of Nineveh without the article, the omission being rhetorically stronger. Raban alone leaves geography for type, taking the Ninevites for those who cease from sin and the queen for those who never learned it, since penitence puts sin away and wisdom shuns it.
43:
Who the possessed man stands for is settled first. Jerome reports a reading he will not take, that the parable describes heretics, in whom the spirit was cast out at their confession of the faith and returned when they went over to heresy; the exposition has a show of learning, he says, but the closing words compel a reference to the Jewish people, so the passage may be consistent throughout. On his own account the spirit went out of the Jews when they received the Law, walked through the wilderness of the Gentiles, and returned when the Gentiles believed and left him nowhere to go — finding the temple empty, since Christ had said “Arise, let us go hence” (John 14:31). Chrysostom reads that history differently: they were possessed while they worshipped idols and slew their sons to demons, the demon was cast out by the prophets, and a worse calamity followed the greater crime of killing Christ; and he applies it beyond them: if we are delivered and then possessed by the same wickedness the later punishment is heavier, as at John 5:14. Augustine takes it of individuals who believe but lack strength for continence and return to the world, gaining a sevenfold hypocrisy over the old lust. John Gill keeps both open: the spirit left the nation in some sort while Christ and the Gospel continued, and he goes out of men whenever an outward reformation is made without the grace of God.

The dry places are read three ways. Albert Barnes and Charles Ellicott take them for literal deserts, referring the language to the current belief that spirits inhabited waterless regions; Adam Clarke adds the classification behind it, demons divided by region into celestial, aerial, aquatic, terrestrial and subterranean. Remigius makes them the hearts of the Gentiles, dry for want of the Scriptures and the Spirit, where the devil expected rest for ever and found none once they believed. Raban and Gregory invert that exactly: the dry places are the hearts of the faithful, dried by discipline of every humour of carnal lust so that the devil can fix no footstep there, while the wet places are the minds of worldly men, marshy ground where his tread sinks deeper. Gregory adds that a soul lifted up early and priding itself on its virtues opens the entrance itself, and the adversary breaks in the more violently for having been cast out even briefly.

On the three words for the house they divide again. Albert Barnes keeps them literal: the man restored to his right mind, in a lucid interval. Adam Clarke and John Wesley read them of a soul that has lost the life of godliness: empty of God, swept of love and meekness and all the fruits of the Spirit, garnished with levity and security, or with the trifles of fashion and the smart speeches they often affect. Raban assigns each a stage: empty of good works through sloth, swept of old vices by baptism, garnished with feigned virtues through hypocrisy. Charles Ellicott gives them a double reference, to the man delivered from frenzy but left to conventional morality with nothing higher to guard him, and to the nation he typifies. John Calvin presses the metaphor the other way: it comes from men who like their apartments neat, whereas to Satan no sight is beautiful but deformity, so he finds no better lodging than the emptiness left when we have parted with Christ.

A.T. Robertson and John Wesley both catch the tone of the returning spirit, who speaks as though he had left of his own accord, like a man stepping out for a walk. Adam Clarke adds an argument of another kind: had possession been a vulgar error, the scribes would have treated the appeal with contempt, and Christ would scarcely have chosen so unreal a case to describe their coming desolation.
45:
What the number stands for is the first question. John Gill offers three possibilities at once: an allusion in mockery to the seven spirits before the throne, or a large number, seven standing for completeness, or the swarms of inward corruption a man carries. Albert Barnes and Adam Clarke settle on the second, Clarke deriving the sense of a thing filled up from the Hebrew and applying it to as many demons as could occupy a soul, harassing it with pride, anger, self-will and lust while the body is tortured with disease. Charles Ellicott takes it for an intensity rather than a count, as in the seven cast out of Mary Magdalene, showing itself in more violent paroxysms and less hope of restoration. John Calvin and John Wesley agree that it is indefinite, and Wesley draws a small inference from the comparative “more wicked” — that there are degrees of wickedness among the devils themselves.

The application to the nation is worked out at different depths. Albert Barnes reads the returning spirit as unbelief made at home: much might be done to cure it and to reform them outwardly, but wickedness had taken such hold as its proper habitation that it would come back and they would grow worse. Charles Ellicott sets out three questions the parable must answer: what corresponds to the first possession and expulsion, what to the seven worse spirits, and what to the last state, still future when Christ spoke. The first lies on the surface of their history, the idolatry that held them from the Exodus to the Captivity and deprived them of light and reason and free will; the expulsion came with the return from exile, when idolatry was banished not so much by the prophets as by the scribes and Pharisees. Adam Clarke reads the ending as already accomplished, since they grew worse until destruction swept away both nation and privileges; and he adds a note on relapse in general, that a soul once dilated under heavenly influence becomes the more capable of refinement in iniquity because its powers are more capacious, evil habits being strengthened by relapses and relapses made more incurable by the habits. John Calvin turns the warning on the reader: if we fall from grace our subjection is doubled and Satan uses us more cruelly, the just reward of our slothfulness; nor must we suppose him vanquished by a single combat because he once went out, for his lodging within us was of old standing, from birth, so that he knows every approach and can creep in by small holes and winding crevices where he cannot enter openly. John Wesley extends the sentence past that generation to apostates in all ages, and marks the finality of the words: they enter in and dwell, in the man forsaken of God.

John Lightfoot alone questions whether the parable can mean what it is usually taken to mean. It can hardly describe spirits cast out by Christ, he argues, since in the whole evangelic history there is not the least shadow of probability that a devil cast out by him ever returned; so the allusion must be to the casting out of devils by exorcism, an art the Jews were well instructed in and which required dexterous deceits and collusions in the practice. On the same footing he doubts the detail about the dry places: it is scarcely credible that the devil truly finds less rest in dry ground than in wet, but very credible that the practitioners of that art invented such figments for its honour and fame. And he adds the reductio, that it would be ridiculous to suppose they could exorcise by their arts a devil whom God himself had sent. What the words do foretell, on his reading, is a dreadful apostasy in that nation and generation.
46:
Who these brethren were is the oldest question here, and it is unsettled. Jerome answers it against Helvidius by distinguishing four scriptural senses of the word — brothers by nature, as Esau and Jacob; by nation, as all Jews (Deuteronomy 17:15); by kindred, as Abraham and Lot (Genesis 13:8); and by affection, whether the special sense in which Christians are brethren (John 20:17) or the general one that binds all men — and denies the first sense here, since Scripture never calls these men sons of Mary or Joseph. John Wesley takes them for kinsmen, the sons of Mary the wife of Cleopas. Against this, Albert Barnes holds the natural meaning to be that they were children of his mother, and finds no valid objection, while A.T. Robertson states it as fact, younger sons of Joseph and Mary. Adam Clarke reports both sides and inclines to the stricter, allowing they may have been sons of Mary’s sister but thinking it as likely they were her own. Charles Ellicott declines to decide: the question cannot be answered with any approximation to certainty, the Greek word having the same latitude as the English and no adequate evidence that it was applied to cousins as such; and though three of the four names in Mark 6:3 recur among the apostles, the statement that his brethren did not believe in him (John 7:5) sets that coincidence aside. Augustine, whatever may be decided about the brethren, will not have sin so much as brought into question in the holy Virgin, for the honour of Christ.

Why they came, and how the answer should be taken, is the second question. Chrysostom reads the timing as the offence: they should have come in and listened with the crowd, or waited for the end of the discourse, and instead they call him out before the multitude, showing both a love of honour and a claim of authority over him. He adds that Christ did not disown her — had he wished to, he would have done it when the Jews threw his birth in his teeth — and that the reply is addressed to the messenger, not to her. A.T. Robertson supplies a gentler motive: some friends thought him beside himself with the strain, so it was natural for his mother to want him home to rest. John Wesley takes that reading too, and Matthew Henry guesses at something similar — that they meant to make him break off for fear of fatigue, or to caution him against giving further offence, as if they could teach him wisdom — noting that he had left the Pharisees but continued with the common people, who were willing to learn. Hilary explains the standing outside differently: they had power to come in like the rest, but abstained from all approach, since he came to his own and his own received him not. Augustine takes the “yet” strictly, fixing the incident to the moment of the foregoing discourse, and notes that Luke placed it earlier without regard to order.

Two of the Latin voices guard the answer from being pressed too far. Ambrose denies that it overthrows the filial duty commanded at Exodus 20:12, holding only that Christ owes more to the mysteries of his Father than to those of his mother. Gregory turns it into a rule for the hearer: a man is made Christ’s brother by coming to the faith and his mother by preaching, since whoever pours him into a hearer’s heart may be said to beget him. He reads the mother standing outside as a figure of the synagogue, unacknowledged by its own Author because it kept to the letter of the Law and stayed outside to guard it. John Gill notes only what was interrupted, a discourse on matters certain to draw the scribes’ resentment.
47:
John Gill thinks the messenger was one of the hearers, or on one reading a disciple, and reconciles the accounts by supposing first one and then several passed the word along, Jesus not going out at once. A.T. Robertson raises a textual question none of the others do: the verse is wanting in the chief early manuscripts and the Old Syriac and is omitted by the modern editors, being genuine at Mark 3:32 and Luke 8:20, whence it was probably copied in.

Why the reply sounds cold is felt by all of them. Albert Barnes denies any want of affection, appealing to the whole life and to Luke 2:51 and John 19:25, and takes the question as a device to fix attention and prepare the hearers; dear as the ties to his mother and brethren were, those to his disciples were nearer — a bright illustration of his own doctrine that a man must leave father and mother to follow him. Adam Clarke gives a blunter reason, that they came to seize him as distracted, and John Wesley that his knowing why they came is justification enough. John Calvin is the least tender: the words reprove Mary’s eagerness, and she acted improperly in trying to break off a discourse while he taught — yet in disparaging the tie of flesh he teaches a most useful doctrine, admitting all believers to the rank of nearest relatives, which belongs to his office, since he was given not to a few but to all the godly made one body with him by faith. Charles Ellicott states the principle rather than the occasion: natural relationships carry duties not to be neglected, but the bond of a common Master stands above them, and where they clash the higher must prevail (Matthew 10:37). A.T. Robertson keeps the human side in view: Jesus loved his mother and brothers but would not have them interfere in his work, and it was hard for Mary to leave him with a throng so pressing he was not stopping to eat (Mark 3:20).

John Gill takes the disciples pointed at to include not the twelve only but all present who truly believed, women as well as men, and A.T. Robertson pictures the wave of the hand that went with the words. John Wesley sets the two halves of the scene against each other as the highest severity and the highest goodness: severity to natural relations who opposed his Father’s will, goodness to spiritual ones who obeyed it. Charles Ellicott turns the saying against the reverence paid to the Virgin Mother in later ages: it excludes the thought that her intercession prevails beyond that of any other saintly soul, and is the stronger protest for being spoken with no reference to such abuses. He notices the mention of a sister too, and suspects those who bore the name had joined in the interruption.

What it is to do the will of the Father is defined narrowly. John Gill denies that perfect obedience to the law is meant, since no mere man performs it and nobody would then stand in this relation to Christ; the sense is the obedience of faith to the will revealed in the Gospel. John Calvin reaches the identical conclusion, that on the stricter reading the name would fit no man living, and that the design is to commend faith, the source of holy obedience, which covers the defects of the flesh so they are not imputed (John 6:40); he adds that Christ observed human order strictly and discharged his duties to relatives, teaching only that by comparison little is due to the flesh. Charles Ellicott makes the test inward, not the fact of baptism but what it signifies, and Adam Clarke draws out the encouragement: whoever does the will of God is esteemed as brother, sister, or even virgin mother.
